scopeReview: CED Topic 1.1 CHA-1.A: instantaneous change interpreted through nonzero shrinking-interval averages. No formal differentiation rules, integration, MVT or BC-only content.
varietyReview: Four numerical rate calculations plus a local-line slope, table estimation, zero-denominator reasoning, units/sign interpretation, disagreement of one-sided rates, limited-data inference and comparison of speed histories. Foundational 3; standard 5; multistep/conceptual challenge 3.
repetitionReview: Each prompt and all four options were read separately; distinct tasks/contexts within this set. Cross-topic exact duplicates checked by validator. Semantic similarity and AP difficulty remain judgment calls, not proven by an automated score.

questions.independentReasoning: An independent unit check and difference calculation give displacement 27 m and duration 3 s. The unique option equal to their ratio is 9 m/s; no constant-speed assumption was made.
optionReview: This is the position change alone; it omits division by the elapsed time.
Correct: the position changes by 27 m during 3 s, giving 9 m/s.
This is the elapsed time, not the change in position divided by time.
This uses an initial position as a rate; a position is not a quotient of changes.

questions.independentReasoning: The deviations from 6 have magnitudes 0.2, 0.02, 0.002 with opposite signs on the two sides. This is an estimation item; the wording deliberately does not claim a finite table proves a limit.
optionReview: Shrinking time intervals do not force their position-change/time-change ratios to approach zero.
The input time 4 s is not a velocity and has different units.
Correct: the short-interval rates on both sides approach 6 m/s.
Adding the two limiting rates double-counts the same local rate.

questions.independentReasoning: The denominator is exactly zero regardless of f(a), including for a nonzero constant function. A line of slope 2 has all nonzero-interval rates 2, disproving the claim that all rates must be zero.
optionReview: An undefined zero-length quotient does not rule out a meaningful instantaneous rate obtained by a limiting process.
Average rates on nonzero intervals can have any sign and need not be zero.
The interval length places no condition on the function value at its endpoint.
Correct: the denominator a−a is zero, so the quotient is undefined.

check.expectedAnswer: The formula divides by a change in the input equal to zero.

questions.independentReasoning: The independent line equation through the supplied points is y=3x−2; it also passes through (4,10). The prompt states the limiting local direction, so it does not infer an exact tangent solely from a distant secant.
optionReview: Correct: the reference line has slope (13−7)/(5−3)=3.
This is the vertical change without division by the horizontal change.
This is the horizontal change, not the slope.
The height of the central point is a function value, not a rate.

questions.independentReasoning: As a separate check, the coefficient of a small time increment for the quadratic at 3 is 2·4·3=24. Substituting h=0.01 and h=−0.01 gives 24.04 and 23.96, consistent with the algebra and a unique numerical choice.
optionReview: This is s(3), the position, and not a rate of change.
Correct: expanding and cancelling gives the average rate 24+4h, which approaches 24.
This keeps only one of the two equal contributions from expanding (3+h)².
Both differences approach zero, but their quotient approaches 24, not zero.

questions.independentReasoning: A line T(t)=20−1.5t has this local rate with noon temperature 20, while T(t)=30−1.5t+t² has the same noon rate but changing later rates. These independent examples eliminate the value and global-constancy distractors.
optionReview: This confuses a rate measured in °C/min with a temperature measured in °C.
Local instantaneous behavior does not impose a constant rate on later intervals.
Correct: the negative sign indicates a decreasing temperature; the magnitude gives the local rate.
Shrinking the intervals need not make the rate quotient approach zero.

check.expectedAnswer: Near noon, temperature is decreasing at approximately 1.5 °C per minute.

questions.independentReasoning: Constructing the line explicitly gives s(t)=12−3t, which returns both supplied positions and changes by −3h over every increment h. Thus the ratio is always −3, not merely an endpoint average.
optionReview: This gives the magnitude but loses the negative direction of the position change.
This is the final position, not a rate.
This uses the change in position without dividing by two seconds.
Correct: a straight position graph has the same slope (6−12)/(2−0)=−3 throughout.

questions.independentReasoning: A continuous broken-line position model with slope 4 before c and −2 after c realizes the data. Each side keeps its own slope on arbitrarily short intervals, so 1 fails both sides and neither one-sided value is common.
optionReview: Correct: two different approaching rates cannot represent one common local rate.
Averaging incompatible side behaviors does not make them approach a common value.
Earlier times do not take priority over the stated right-side behavior.
Later times do not override conflicting behavior from earlier intervals.

check.expectedAnswer: The two sides do not support a single common instantaneous rate at c.

questions.independentReasoning: Independent dimensional arithmetic gives 30/2=15 after scaling numerator and denominator by 100. A nonlinear volume change over the interval can preserve the total 0.30 L while changing either endpoint rate; therefore only the average is guaranteed.
optionReview: Endpoint instantaneous rates are not determined by one interval’s total change.
Correct: the measured ratio is 0.30/0.02=15 L/min for that interval.
The same interval average can occur for functions with different endpoint rates.
A single interval measurement does not establish constant behavior.

check.expectedAnswer: An average rate of 15 liters per minute over the recorded interval

questions.independentReasoning: For a concrete separate model, cyclist one travels 12 m/s throughout; cyclist two travels 8 m/s for the first 10 s and 16 m/s for the last 10 s. Both cover 240 m, but the instantaneous speeds away from the switching time differ.
optionReview: Different speed histories can have the same total distance over the same duration.
The distance/time ratio does not imply constancy.
Correct: equal total distances and durations give equal average speeds without prescribing local behavior.
The data do not force a difference at the start; equal starting speeds are also possible.

check.expectedAnswer: Their average speeds over the interval are equal, but their speeds at a specified instant need not be equal.

questions.independentReasoning: A separate coefficient-of-increment calculation gives 5−2·4=−3. Values h=0.1 and h=−0.1 produce −3.1 and −2.9, checking the sign and distinguishing the positive position from its negative rate.
optionReview: This takes the position p(4) as a velocity.
This discards the negative direction of the approaching rate.
This confuses a quadratic coefficient with the local rate.
Correct: the quotient simplifies to −3−h, whose approaching value is −3.
